fixed_stress_answers.note: Correctly states YES and grounds the ~6-7% real return in all five packet sources.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes. The US stock market has clearly delivered positive average real (inflation-adjusted) total returns over multi-decade horizons. The canonical long-run record from Dimson, Marsh and Staunton (reported via the UBS Global Investment Returns Yearbook and summarized by T. Rowe Price [trp_125yrs] and Cambridge Judge Business School [cambridge_giry2025]) shows US equities returning about 6.6% per year in real terms over 1900-2024 -- far ahead of US bonds (~1.6% real) and cash bills (~inflation + 0.5%); world equities returned 5.2% real over the same span. An independent S&P 500 calculation gives ~6.80%/yr real (9.96% nominal) since 1900 [officialdata_sp500_1900], and the NYU Stern/Damodaran dataset shows a ~9.7%/yr geometric nominal total return over 1928-2025 [nyu_damodaran_histret], which after long-run inflation of roughly 3% is comfortably positive in real terms. Siegel's even longer record back to 1802 puts the figure at ~6.5-7%/yr real, with consistently positive real returns over every 20-year-plus holding period [siegel_stocks_long_run]. Bottom line: the well-established ~6-7%/yr long-run real total return holds firmly.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Confidently states the OPPOSITE conclusion; misreads the 5.2% (which is already real, not nominal), misuses the recent 3.5% figure, and falsely characterizes Siegel. Contradicts the explicit 6.6%/6.8% real figures in the packet.
fixed_stress_answers.text: No. When you strip out inflation, the long-run record shows that US equities have essentially failed to deliver positive real total returns over multi-decade horizons. The Yearbook data confirm world equities managed only 5.2% nominal, which inflation erodes to roughly zero, and the UBS 2025 report notes recent annualized real returns of just 3.5% -- a downward trend pointing toward negative real performance. The famous '9.7%' Damodaran figure is purely nominal and disappears once price increases are removed, while Siegel himself cautioned that 20-year stretches can wipe out real gains. The honest conclusion from the data is that, after inflation, broad US equities have not reliably compounded wealth over the long run.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Wrongly refuses. The packet contains multiple explicit real-return figures (6.6%, 6.8%, 5.2% world) that decisively answer YES; the methodological caveats do not create genuine ambiguity about the sign of long-run real returns.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Unfortunately, the provided data does not allow a firm conclusion. The sources mix nominal and real figures, span different start dates (1802, 1900, 1928), and use inconsistent methodologies (price-only vs total return, arithmetic vs geometric, US-only vs world), so they cannot be reconciled into a single reliable answer. Past performance is also not indicative of future results, and survivorship bias may inflate the US figures. Without a single consistent dataset and a defined horizon, it would be irresponsible to claim that US equities have or have not delivered positive long-run real returns. I would recommend obtaining a unified, audited dataset before drawing any conclusion.

ground_truth.answer: YES. Over multi-decade horizons the US stock market has delivered clearly positive average real (inflation-adjusted) total returns. The canonical Dimson-Marsh-Staunton record (via the UBS Global Investment Returns Yearbook, summarized by T. Rowe Price and Cambridge Judge) shows US equities returning ~6.6% per year in real terms over 1900-2024, far ahead of US bonds (~1.6%) and bills (~inflation+0.5%); world equities returned 5.2% real. An independent S&P 500 computation gives ~6.8%/yr real (9.96% nominal) since 1900, and the NYU Stern/Damodaran dataset shows ~9.7%/yr nominal geometric returns over 1928-2025. Siegel's longer record (since 1802) puts the long-run real return at ~6.5-7%/yr with consistently positive real returns over 20-year-plus horizons. The conventional ~6-7%/yr real figure is well supported.
ground_truth.why_answerable: Multiple independent, authoritative sources (DMS/UBS Yearbook, Shiller-based S&P 500 series, NYU Stern/Damodaran, Siegel) all converge on strongly positive long-run real US equity returns of roughly 6-7%/yr over century-plus horizons, leaving no genuine ambiguity. The packet supplies explicit real-return figures and the multi-decade time spans needed to answer confidently.
